analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal rules on for-profit colleges and expands protections for student borrowers.
analysis.headline: The PRO Students Act, a House bill to tighten rules on for-profit colleges and expand student borrower protections, died in committee with just 4 cosponsors and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have imposed new rules on for-profit colleges, which live almost entirely on federal student aid. It would have required them to draw at least 15% of revenue from non-federal sources or lose federal aid, banned them from using federal aid dollars for recruiting and advertising, barred forced-arbitration clauses in enrollment and loan-servicing contracts, and made it easier for misled students to have their federal loans wiped out. It also would have created a federal complaint hotline for students, protected whistleblowers at the schools, and let the Education Department fine abusive schools and put the penalties into a fund that repays students.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and prospective students at for-profit colleges — many of them low-income, first-generation, veteran, and working-adult students — would gain protections against aggressive recruiting, inflated job claims, and forced arbitration. Student borrowers who were misled by a school would have broader grounds to cancel their federal loans, and an expanded borrower-defense process would require the Education Department to cancel qualifying debt and return payments. Employees and contractors at the schools would get whistleblower protection, and all students would get a single federal hotline and public complaint records for each school.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and borrowers at for-profit colleges

how_it_helps.text: For-profit colleges would have to draw at least 15% of their revenue from non-federal sources or become ineligible for federal student aid, tightening the existing 90-10 rule and closing accounting loopholes that let schools count their own institutional loans and scholarships as non-federal revenue.

The bill would prohibit colleges from using federal student aid dollars for recruiting and marketing, and require schools that get 65% or more of their revenue from federal aid to report their marketing spending with independent auditor verification.

It would ban predispute arbitration clauses in enrollment contracts and in federal loan servicing contracts, so students and borrowers could not be forced to give up their right to sue the school or the servicer.

It would broaden borrower defenses to repayment, letting students assert substantial misrepresentation or any claim allowed under state law, and requiring the Education Department to cancel outstanding debt and return payments when a borrower qualifies.

It would create a toll-free complaint system for students and families, publish complaint data for each school, protect whistleblowers at the institutions, establish a multi-agency oversight committee for for-profit colleges, and publish an annual 'Warning List for Parents and Students' of schools with records of fraudulent or predatory practices.

The Education Department could impose civil penalties of at least $100,000 and up to millions on schools that substantially misrepresent their programs, and at least half of penalty collections would go into a Student Relief Fund providing tuition reimbursement or loan forgiveness to harmed students.

It would crack down on 'default manipulation' — tactics schools use to make their student loan default rates look better — by requiring the Department to recalculate manipulated default rates and redetermine the school's aid eligibility.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges would bear the main costs: compliance with the tighter revenue test and disclosure rules, a ban on using federal aid for recruiting and advertising, potential civil penalties, and loss of federal aid eligibility if they failed the 15% non-federal revenue test. Loan servicers and debt collectors would lose the ability to force borrowers into arbitration, and colleges could no longer shield themselves from lawsuits with arbitration clauses in enrollment contracts. Taxpayers would fund the complaint system and oversight committee, though penalty collections would partially offset that.

drawbacks.text: The stricter 85-15 revenue test and civil penalties could push marginal for-profit schools out of business, and when a school closes abruptly its current students can be left stranded mid-program with credits that may not transfer — a cost the bill does not directly address for students already enrolled.

The bill imposes new compliance burdens on all institutions, not just bad actors: annual certification, disclosure of clinical training agreements with hospitals, complaints response deadlines, and public reporting requirements that nonprofit and public colleges would also have to meet.
The bill's new two-week enrollment waiting period and expanded disclosures for schools with high default risk could slow down enrollment for adult students who need to start a program quickly.

Most of the protections depend on the Education Department actively enforcing them — the bill authorizes appropriations 'as may be necessary' for some functions rather than guaranteeing funding, so a passive administration could leave the complaint system and penalties underused.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students and borrowers, the protections — loan cancellation for misled students, a ban on forced arbitration, a complaint hotline, and penalties that fund student relief — are substantial, and the main costs fall on the for-profit college industry rather than the public. The honest trade-off is that the rules most likely to close bad schools can also strand the students currently enrolled at them, and the whole scheme works only if the Education Department chooses to enforce it aggressively. On balance, the bill's benefits for students would have outweighed those costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the Protections and Regulation for Our Students Act in the House on June 25, 2019.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor — the standard first step — and four House Democrats signed on as cosponsors.
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor; the complete action history shows no action after the referral, so the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges and student loan servicers came out ahead: none of the new restrictions, penalties, or disclosure requirements took effect, so the industry kept operating under the existing rules.

for.name: Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PRO Students Act, which tightened oversight of for-profit colleges and expanded student borrower protections.

for.name: 4 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it drew no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral on June 25, 2019 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll call shows party positions; its only supporters on the record were Democrats (one sponsor and four of 231 House Democratic cosponsors), and the Democratic-controlled committee declined to advance it.

industries.note: The bill targets this industry's core business model: for-profit schools would have had to secure 15% of revenue from non-federal sources or lose federal student aid, could no longer spend federal aid dollars on recruiting and advertising, faced civil penalties for misrepresentation, and would appear on an annual federal warning list. Because these schools depend heavily on federal aid, the restrictions would have cut directly into enrollment growth and marketing budgets. Its death left the industry's rules unchanged.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: Federal loan servicing contracts would have had to include a provision barring forced-arbitration clauses that waive borrowers' rights, exposing servicers to lawsuits they can currently avoid. The bill died, so servicers kept the status quo.

industries.industry: Recruitment marketing and lead-generation firms serving colleges
industries.note: The bill would have banned colleges from paying for lead generation, paid search ads aimed at capturing student contact information, and other recruiting activities using federal aid dollars — a revenue stream for companies that funnel prospective students to for-profit schools. With no action on the bill, those arrangements continued.
